summary:
Consensual sex between men is a criminal offence in Kenya. Section 162 of the Penal Code makes carnal knowledge against the order of nature a felony punishable by up to 14 years' imprisonment, rising to 21 years where the act is committed without consent or where consent is obtained by force, threats, fear of bodily harm or false representations as to the nature of the act. Section 163 punishes an attempt with 7 years, and section 165 punishes acts of gross indecency between males with 5 years. The provisions apply regardless of the nationality of those involved. In 2019 the High Court declined to declare sections 162 and 165 unconstitutional in Eric Gitari v Attorney General (Petition 150 of 2016); the Court of Appeal hearing was scheduled for May 2026 and a decision is pending.

No Kenyan statute governs gender identity, and there is no codified pathway for legal gender recognition. Intersex people are legally recognised as a third gender, according to the UK Home Office country policy and information note of February 2025.

On 20 May 2026 the Milimani High Court in Nairobi ruled that Kenyans must be allowed to change gender markers on identification documents. The decision, delivered by Justice Bahati Mwamuye in Petition 27 of 2020, followed a suit filed in 2020 by the transgender activist Audrey Mbugua and two others seeking to amend birth certificates. Evidence before the court showed that 94 per cent of trans and gender-diverse Kenyans had been refused by civil registration offices, with some applicants spending close to four years' wages on document corrections that failed.

On 12 August 2025 the Eldoret High Court directed the state to enact a Transgender Protection Rights Act, finding that prisons fail to protect the dignity and privacy of transgender detainees. The petition came from a transgender Kenyan who was subjected to nonconsensual medical procedures and a court-ordered gender determination during incarceration. In the same month the High Court found that violations of a specific transgender person's rights, including freedom from torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, equality and non-discrimination, dignity, freedom and security of the person, and privacy, were unconstitutional, and ordered parliament to enact the Transgender Protection Rights Act or, in the alternative, to amend the Intersex Persons Bill 2024.

Police treatment of transgender people is documented as routine rather than exceptional. Interviews with 26 trans and intersex people in Mombasa and Nairobi recorded detention on pretexts such as drunk and disorderly, on-the-spot extortion with demands such as "look for 5,000 shillings", and the use of traditionally male names as pseudonyms to move through society safely. The Kenya Human Rights Commission in 2011 and the National Gay and Lesbian Human Rights Commission in 2020 and 2021 reported routine police harassment, detention in remand beyond the constitutional period without charge, presentation on trumped-up charges, extortion and blackmail for bribes, demands for bribes and sexual favours from men who have sex with men, and rape by state security officers.

On 22 March 2018 the Court of Appeal in Mombasa ruled forced anal examinations on persons accused of same-sex relations unconstitutional, reversing a 2016 High Court decision. Police in February 2015 had arrested two men in Kwale County and subjected them to forced anal examinations and HIV and hepatitis B tests at Mombasa's Madaraka Hospital; a later anal examination was halted by the Kangundo magistrate court for two men taken from Kakuyuni to Kangundo Level 4 hospital. Compensation in the forced-testing litigation was awarded in 2024.

Violence against sexual and gender minorities is documented and in at least one case prosecuted. In December 2024 a Kenyan man was sentenced to 50 years in jail for killing an LGBTQ activist. The Kenya Human Rights Commission's September 2025 report Lives on the Line is the first comprehensive documentation of human-rights violations against sexual and gender minorities in Kenya, covering October 2023 to September 2024, and it challenges the 2019 High Court ruling in Petition 16 of 2019 that dismissed LGBTIQ+ violence claims for purported lack of evidence.

Article 45(2) of the Constitution, in force since 27 August 2010, authorises marriage only between a man and a woman, and no legal recognition exists for a relationship the state classifies as same-sex, which is the classification a trans visitor's relationship would attract where the couple's recorded birth sexes match. The Children Act 2001 makes homosexuals and unmarried couples ineligible to adopt.

There are no explicit protections against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Article 27(4) and (5) non-discrimination provisions are argued to allow claims on sexual orientation grounds, and the government agreed with that interpretation in a May 2012 submission to the United Nations.

Two custody and facilities risks follow from the absence of gender recognition. Police face difficulty deciding whether to detain transgender individuals in male or female cells when arrested. Transgender people also report fearing the use of sex-designated bathrooms in entertainment areas, for fear of being accused of using bathrooms for sexual crimes.
tangentialFactors:
The Family Protection Bill, introduced in 2023 by the MP George Peter Opondo Kaluma under file reference DLS/NA/BILLS/2/18/2023, would allow aggravated homosexuality to be punished with death, criminalise all promotion of LGBTQ+ activity, restrict privacy, assembly and public demonstration, prohibit pride parades, provide for monitoring of private and public spaces, remove LGBTQ+ topics from school curricula, and overturn the 2023 Supreme Court decision affirming the right to form associations. It has remained stalled before the Committee on Social Protection for close to two years.

In responses to the ICCPR and the Universal Periodic Review between 2010 and 2012, the government said it would not decriminalise same-sex unions, describing them as taboo and culturally unacceptable, while stating that it did not support discrimination in access to services, including HIV/AIDS prevention under the 2006 Act.

Access to HIV services has been contested locally: in February 2010 religious leaders in Mtwapa demanded the closure of a KEMRI HIV research institute.

Court-driven change has been uneven. The 2018 Mombasa Court of Appeal ruling against forced anal testing, the 2023 Supreme Court decision upholding freedom of association and allowing LGBTQ organisation registration, and a petition filed against incitement to hatred and discrimination sit alongside the 2019 High Court refusal to strike down the criminal provisions and the 2019 dismissal of violence claims in Petition 16 of 2019.
localsOnly:
Access to transition-related care is obstructed. The Kenya National Commission on Human Rights reported in April 2012 that transgender people are unable to access gender reassignment therapy; a witness who had completed all required processes was declined surgery by Kenyatta National Hospital without reasons, and an appeal to the Kenya Medical Practitioners and Dentist's Board was unsuccessful.

Societal discrimination reaches employment and education. A US State Department human rights report for the 2010 reporting year recorded widespread discrimination based on sexual orientation causing loss of employment and education, while organisations such as the Gay and Lesbian Coalition of Kenya were permitted to register and operate.

Transgender Kenyans face stigma, discrimination and violence, with discrimination and sexual violence reported in areas including government recognition of a third sex, access to justice, employment and other spheres of public life. A documented risk arises on disclosure: when partners demanding sexual relationships discover that a person is not female or male, they have screamed and drawn members of the public to the hotel room, causing public nuisance, stigma and embarrassment to the transgender person.

Community infrastructure exists but operates under pressure. The Lives on the Line report was built with more than 14 community organisations, and active LGBTIQ+ organisations raise awareness and provide community spaces amid documented violence. The Star reported that the report used purposive sampling of organisations active in advocacy, data and service provision, and that despite the dignity guarantee in Article 28 of the Constitution, the data paints a blunt picture.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Transgender Protection Rights Act directed by the High Court in August 2025 has been enacted is not established by the sources reviewed; the directive and the alternative route of amending the Intersex Persons Bill 2024 remain the recorded outcome.

The Court of Appeal hearing on the constitutionality of sections 162 and 165 was scheduled for May 2026 with the decision pending, so the appellate position on the criminal provisions is unresolved.

The Family Protection Bill's current status is unresolved: it is recorded as stalled before the Committee on Social Protection for close to two years, with no sourced vote or withdrawal.

Some evidence is dated. The US State Department report covers the 2010 reporting year and the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights findings date from April 2012; both describe conditions that later court rulings and the 2025 Kenya Human Rights Commission report address only in part.

Sample limitations are not resolved by the sources. The police-harassment account rests on interviews with 26 people in two cities, and the Lives on the Line report used purposive sampling of organisations active in advocacy, data and service provision, so neither is a population-level measure.
